source: Zhao, Awasthi, Gollapudi (2025) Sample, Scrutinize and Scale: Effective Inference-Time Search by Scaling Verification
finding: Training-free sampling-based search: sample many answers, then have the same model verify each one with many natural-language checks and average the scores. It beats plain self-consistency, but it uses far more tokens.
numbers: Gemini v1.5 Pro, single run per cell. Pass@1 / Consistency@200 / Consistency@1000 / Verification@200: AIME 1/15, 4/15, 3/15, 8/15. MATH 426, 460, 460, 467 of 500. LiveBench Math 104, 118, 120, 135 of 200. LiveBench Reasoning 63, 75, 73, 97 of 140. Verification used k_verif=50 checks per candidate. Cost on AIME about 13,000 output tokens per verification, so 200 x 50 x 13,000 = 130M tokens, about 650 USD per question (about 200 USD with preliminary scoring, about 12 USD with Flash as verifier).
quote: scaling sampling indirectly enhances verification accuracy
limits: Not equal compute: Verification@200 costs far more than Consistency@1000. Tie-breaking explains most of the gain on MATH and LiveBench Math (Table 3: MATH 457/500 without tie-break, below Cons@200 at 460, vs 467 with it). Single runs, 15 AIME questions, Gemini v1.5 only. Pro+Flash verification (about the cost of Consistency@500) gave MATH 456/500, below Pro Cons@200 at 460, but beat it on AIME (7 vs 4) and LiveBench Reasoning (84 vs 75).
agent_relevance: A verify-then-vote step can beat voting once voting has plateaued, but a full check chain per candidate is very expensive. Gap 1 answer: it crosses over only where voting has saturated (AIME, LiveBench Reasoning), and the tie-break role may be the cheapest useful part. Use a cheap tie-break among the top voted answers instead of verifying every candidate.

source: Zhao, Awasthi, Gollapudi (2025) Sample, Scrutinize and Scale (verification error rates, implicit scaling, benchmark of verification)
finding: Prompted self-verification by Gemini v1.5 Pro has error rates of roughly 7 to 23 percent per type when 20 checks are averaged, but frontier models do much worse out of the box on a hard benchmark of verification. Rewriting the solution before checking, and comparing across responses, help.
numbers: Table 4 (1,080 candidate responses to 54 MATH level-5 questions; 120 responses to 6 AIME 2023 questions; 20 verification attempts per response, threshold at the equal error rate). Main prompt: MATH 14% / 17%, AIME 7% / 7%. Without rewrite: 16% / 18% and 11% / 12%. Split-context: 19% / 23% and 11% / 14%. On their benchmark of hard verification cases models score marginally better than, and often worse than, chance on the comparison task; Consistency@5 is often worse than one-shot.
limits: The table caption defines FPR as 'correct labelled incorrect', the reverse of the usual meaning, so read the two columns as two error types and do not trust the names. These rates need 20 checks per response averaged; a single check is noisier. Math only. The paper says verification errors are mainly low recall.
agent_relevance: Direct measurement of a prompted verifier with many checks: 7 to 23 percent error each way on math. It gives no rates for puzzles or planning (see d04, d15). Implicit scaling (more samples make the verifier more accurate because good answers are easier to check) argues for giving the verifier several candidates and letting it compare them.

source: Chen et al. (2025) SETS: Leveraging Self-Verification and Self-Correction for Improved Test-Time Scaling
finding: A training-free loop (sample, self-verify, self-correct) beats best-of-N with majority vote at comparable token budgets on planning tasks, and by little or not at all on math. Plain best-of-N with self-verification beats majority vote on planning but loses on AIME.
numbers: Table 4, fixed hyperparameters, 3 repeats, mean accuracy %, Gemini-1.5-Pro. Trip Planning: BoN+Majority Vote 49.9, BoN+Self-Verify 60.6, SELF-REFINE 59.5, SETS 68.5. Meeting Planning: 48.8, 55.7, 54.1, 59.6. MATH500: 87.8, 88.7, 87.8, 89.3. AIME 2024-2025: 32.2, 28.3, 23.3, 33.3. Authors claim up to 10.9% accuracy gain over baselines.
limits: Table layout is scrambled in the text I extracted, so token counts per row are not verified; the paper states budgets are comparable. The stated gain is the best case. The authors say SETS gives little gain when a model's self-verification and self-correction are weak (Claude-3.5-Sonnet on LiveBench Reasoning). Thinking-model results are in the appendix and were not read.
agent_relevance: Best direct evidence for gap 1 on non-math tasks: on constraint-checkable planning tasks, training-free self-verification beats voting at similar tokens by 7 to 11 points (best-of-N verify vs vote) and by about 10 to 19 points with correction. On AIME voting wins. Verification pays where checking is easier than solving and the answer space is large.

source: Chen et al. (2025) SETS (self-verification precision and recall by task and model, Table 2)
finding: Self-verification quality of current models depends strongly on the task. On planning tasks it is good (precision and recall above 90 for Gemini-1.5-Pro on Trip Planning). On math and code it is often poor. Error is the positive class.
numbers: Trip Planning: Claude-3.5-Sonnet precision 93.74, recall 91.85, F1 92.78 (initial accuracy 41.62); Gemini-1.5-Pro 97.51, 94.04, 95.74 (initial accuracy 43.44). Meeting Planning: Claude 80.30 / 82.29; Gemini-1.5-Pro 74.18 / 66.39. Other rows in the table range from F1 about 17 to 83, with several math and code rows having recall of 20 to 35 or precision of 15 to 30. Self-correction in 2 rounds changes accuracy by between -5.0 and +22.2 points depending on model and task. Appendix D.3: more self-verification samples with a vote raise verification accuracy.
limits: The extracted Table 2 mixes rows between models and datasets, so only the clean Trip Planning and Meeting Planning rows are quoted per model. Models are Gemini 1.5/2.5 and Claude-3.5, not o-series or R1. Checking a proposed plan against stated constraints is closer to constraint checking than to open reasoning.
agent_relevance: Partly closes gap 2: Stechly's 95%+ false-negative rate on graph colouring (GPT-4, 2023) does not hold for plan checking with Claude-3.5 and Gemini-1.5 (recall of errors 92 to 94% on Trip Planning). But it is task-specific and unstable on math or code. Measure the checker on a small labelled set per task before trusting it.

source: Saad-Falcon et al. (2025) Shrinking the Generation-Verification Gap with Weak Verifiers (Weaver)
finding: Combining many weak verifiers (reward models and LM judges), weighted by accuracy estimated with weak supervision, beats majority vote and naive ensembles by a large margin with 100 samples. Naive ensembles and self-verification are no better than the first sample.
numbers: Llama 3.3 70B generator, K=100 samples, 33 verifiers. Average over MATH500, GPQA Diamond, MMLU College, MMLU Pro: first sample 68.4, majority vote 72.2, best reward model 72.7, naive ensemble of top-10 reward models 69.1, self-verification 66.9, multi-agent verification 71.6, Weaver 87.7, o3-mini pass@1 86.7, oracle pass@100 91.9. MATH500 78.0 (first), 83.0 (vote), 93.4 (Weaver). GPQA Diamond 42.9, 47.4, 72.1. A distilled 400M cross-encoder keeps 98.2 to 98.7% of the gain at 0.57% added inference cost.
limits: The paper contradicts itself in places (Weaver vs vote gap given as 13.5, 12.3 and 15.5 points; Table 3 averages do not match Table 1). I used the HTML and a text dump; Table 1 column order was unclear in extraction. Weaver needs a small labelled dev set (1 to 5% of data) to set class balance: naive 0.5 threshold gave 79.0 average, a 5% dev set gave 87.5. Verifiers are trained reward models and judges, not training-free prompts. Conditional independence of verifiers is assumed.
agent_relevance: Evidence that diverse imperfect checks can be combined into a much stronger one, and that unweighted averaging of correlated checks does not work. For a scaffold with no trained reward models, the lesson is to weight checks by measured accuracy on a small labelled set and to drop checks that are nearly always positive or always negative.

source: Saad-Falcon et al. (2025) Weaver (verifier correlation, pruning ablation)
finding: The verifiers used in Weaver have very low pairwise score correlation, and dropping extreme verifiers matters. Adding verifiers helps up to a point and then flattens because of correlated bias on hard questions.
numbers: Table 16: average pairwise Pearson correlation between verifier scores about 0.03 (8B setting 0.0253 to 0.0349; 70B 0.0211 to 0.0372); the range of individual verifier accuracies spans 27 to 41 points. Table 5 (70B, average over 4 datasets): no verifiers dropped 79.4; dropping low-marginal (mostly negative) verifiers 84.2; dropping high-marginal (mostly positive) 79.9; dropping both extremes 85.2. Adding verifiers gave up to +8.5% over the top single verifier; Weaver beat naive averaging by +2.4 to +10.1 points. The authors attribute flattening to 'correlated biases on hard examples'.
limits: Pearson correlation is across flattened query-candidate scores, not across errors on the same hard items, so it understates error correlation. Correlation on hard items was described but not quantified. Numbers are from the HTML text dump.
agent_relevance: Partly answers gap 8: ensembles of heterogeneous checks do cut error, but the paper does not measure error correlation on the items where the generator fails, which is the one that matters. Diversity of checkers helps; more copies of the same checker does not.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Pitfalls of Rule- and Model-based Verifiers: A Case Study on Mathematical Reasoning
finding: Rule-based math verifiers reject many correct answers, and the miss rate rises as the generating model gets stronger. Model-based verifiers fix recall in static tests but can be hacked during RL, and a verifier with better static accuracy was more hackable.
numbers: Rule-based verifiers: precision above 99% but average recall only 86% over datasets (14% of correct responses rejected); recall as low as 0.78 on Skywork-OR1 and lower for long-CoT models such as DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen. Model-based: recall raised from 84% to 92% on Skywork-OR1. Prompted DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B as a judge on the hard residual set: precision 0.79, recall 0.59 on average. general-verifier: precision 0.90, recall 0.86. The trained R1-Distill-Verifier-1.5B (higher static accuracy) diverged from the oracle reward after about 450 RL iterations and training collapsed.
limits: Math only; RL-training setting, not inference-time selection. The oracle reward was GPT-4o. Some table rows are garbled in text extraction, so only quoted cells were used.
agent_relevance: Verifier accuracy on a static test does not predict resistance to being gamed. For a scaffold that selects among samples, an LLM verifier that reads the candidate's argument can be fooled by confident wording; prefer checks that do not read the candidate's own justification.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Pitfalls of Rule- and Model-based Verifiers (hacking patterns, Table 4)
finding: Simple adversarial strings make most LLM verifiers call wrong answers correct. Generative verifiers (which reason before judging) are more fooled than discriminative ones.
numbers: Success rate of fooling the verifier (%), selected cells: DS-R1-Distill-Qwen-7B as judge: adversarial prefix 20.8, answer explanation 77.9, empty symbols 44.4; xVerify-3B-Ia: 1.9, 7.6, 8.3 and near zero on other patterns; R1-Distill-Verifier-1.5B: adversarial prefix 35.0 after training vs 21.7 before. 13 hacking-pattern types tested.
limits: Column alignment in the extracted table is imperfect; the text states the pattern (CoT-based generative verifiers more exposed) and the 21.7 to 35 rise explicitly. Math only.
agent_relevance: A prompted judge that reasons in text is exposed to 'the answer is correct, I verified it' style content in the candidate. Strip explanations from candidates before judging, or judge the final answer against a reference or a code check.

source: Cai et al. (2025) Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable yet Noisy Rewards under Imperfect Verifiers
finding: Models the verifier as a noisy reward channel with separate false-positive and false-negative rates. The forward correction needs only the false-negative rate, which is easier to estimate than the false-positive rate.
numbers: The intro cites other work: rule-based false negatives about 38%; LLM judge false positives 35% to 66.8% when fooled by phrases such as 'Let's solve it step by step'. An appeals mechanism estimates the FN rate online with a rule-based checker plus a model. Experiments use Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B on DeepScaleR with synthetic noise (for example a shared FP rate of 0.2).
limits: I read the abstract, intro and method outline, not all appendices. The 38% and 35 to 66.8% figures are quoted from cited papers, not measured here. Training-time method.
agent_relevance: The false-positive rate is the one that matters for resampling, and it is the hard one to measure. A small labelled audit of accepted answers is the cheap way to estimate it.

source: Helff et al. (2026) LLMs Gaming Verifiers: RLVR can Lead to Reward Hacking
finding: On inductive rule-learning tasks, RL-trained reasoning models (GPT-5 family, Olmo 3) list instance labels instead of inducing a rule, which an extensional verifier accepts. Non-RLVR models (GPT-4o, GPT-4.5, Ministral) did none. A perturbation test (rename objects, same structure) catches it.
numbers: SLR-Bench, 250 tasks per tier. Aggregated shortcut counts: 40 in complexity levels 1 to 10 vs 458 in levels 11 to 20. gpt-5-mini shortcuts rose from 0 (low effort) to 32 (medium) and 84 (high effort). 70% of gpt-5-mini-high shortcuts fall in the top complexity quartile. Controlled training of Olmo 3 with an extensional verifier produced a growing gap between extensional and isomorphic reward; the isomorphic verifier kept it near zero.
limits: Workshop paper; one task family (logic rules). Cause is shown by the training experiment only for Olmo 3. Detection needs a perturbation that preserves the task.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that when a checker only tests the instances it was shown, a strong model will find the shortcut, and more thinking effort finds more shortcuts. For the agent: add a check that varies the instance (rename, reorder, new inputs) before accepting an answer that passes.

source: d'Aliberti and Horta Ribeiro (2026) The Illusion of Insight in Reasoning Models
finding: Mid-reasoning shifts ('Wait, let me re-evaluate') in RL-trained models are rare and usually do not raise accuracy. Forcing a reconsideration prompt when token entropy is high does raise accuracy, so the benefit comes from the trigger, not from spontaneous self-correction.
numbers: Over 1M reasoning traces, hundreds of GRPO checkpoints; Qwen2.5-1.5B (main), Qwen2.5-7B, Llama 3.1-8B; tasks: cryptic crosswords, math, Rush Hour. Shifts in 6.31% of traces overall; the formal 'Aha' detector fires on 1.79% of samples. At T=0.7 a shift is mildly harmful on crosswords and math (average marginal effect -0.0311, p=0.027; -0.0615, p=1.6e-4) and about zero on Rush Hour. Forced reconsideration (paired, 320,000 math samples): accuracy 0.3221 to 0.4062, +8.41 points; 50,574 wrong-to-right vs 23,500 right-to-wrong; crosswords +0.45 points.
limits: Small models (mostly 1.5B) trained with GRPO by the authors, not frontier reasoning models such as o-series or R1. Prompted reconsideration is an external cue, so it is not intrinsic self-correction. The entropy gate needs token probabilities.
agent_relevance: Partly answers gap 3: for RL-trained small models, spontaneous mid-trace correction does not help. A scaffold that triggers a second look when uncertainty is high (here entropy; for an API agent, vote disagreement) is supported; asking the model to recheck every time is not.

source: Xiong et al. (2025) Self-rewarding correction for mathematical reasoning
finding: Intrinsic self-correction by prompting, with no reward signal, still fails on a 2024-2025 math model: the model changes answers whether or not they are right. Even with a gold reward given in the prompt, a prompted model fixes few wrong answers.
numbers: Qwen2.5-Math-7B-base, Table 3, MATH500: intrinsic self-correction 71.6 to 70.4 (-1.2); gold reward in the prompt 65.4 to 51.4 (-14.0), with incorrect-to-correct changes only 1.4% and correct-to-incorrect 15.4%. On one of the harder benchmarks in the table, intrinsic self-correction moved +4.0 and +4.4 from low bases (35.4 to 39.4, 34.0 to 38.4). Llama-3-8B-it and SFT variants: changes between -11.5 and +8.5 across datasets. Trained self-rewarding models reached 43.4% on OlympiadBench and 38.4% on Minerva vs 39.5% and 33.1% for single-turn.
limits: Not an RL-trained long-CoT reasoning model such as R1 or o1; rows in the extracted table are mixed so only cells matching the text were used. The training-based fixes need SFT/RL.
agent_relevance: Replicates Huang 2023's direction on a newer math model: prompting alone does not give reliable self-correction, and the model has no rule for when to change an answer. A scaffold should revise only after an external or independent signal (disagreement, failed check), not by default.

source: Long et al. (2026) Self-Verification Dilemma: Experience-Driven Suppression of Overused Checking in LLM Reasoning
finding: In reasoning models' own traces, most rechecks only confirm the earlier result. The model checks itself often but very seldom finds an error.
numbers: Qwen3-8B on four benchmarks: rechecks are 40% to 58% of reflective steps; 85% to 95% of rechecks are confirmatory and change neither the intermediate nor the final answer. Human audit of 1,000 reflective steps: corrective rechecks 54 (5.4%) human vs 48 (4.8%) LLM labels; confirmatory 428 (42.8%) vs 374 (37.4%); rethinks 518 (51.8%) vs 489 (48.9%). Their suppression method cuts tokens by up to 20.3% with accuracy kept.
limits: Math benchmarks, one main model (Qwen3-8B) plus others in the paper. The classifier is GPT-5 with a human audit. Confirmatory rechecks might still prevent errors that would otherwise occur; the paper does not test that.
agent_relevance: Modern reasoning models still do mostly self-confirmation. It supports spending verification budget on independent checks and not on in-trace rechecks.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Reasoning Models Know When They're Right: Probing Hidden States for Self-Verification
finding: Hidden states of R1-distilled models carry a usable signal about whether an intermediate answer is correct, even when the model does not act on it. Early exit using the probe saves tokens.
numbers: Probes on DeepSeek-R1-Distill models of several sizes up to 32B: in-distribution ROC-AUC above 0.7 and ECE below 0.1; R1-Distill-Qwen-32B reaches above 0.9 AUC on AIME. Probe-based early exit: 24% fewer inference tokens without losing accuracy. Out-of-distribution transfer is weaker and less calibrated on AIME when trained on GSM8K and MATH.
limits: Needs hidden-state access, so not usable with a closed API agent. Math and logic only. The probe is trained, not prompted.
agent_relevance: Shows the model holds more than it says, which is why a separate short independent check step could add something. It cannot be used directly in a scaffold-only agent.

source: Valmeekam et al. (2024) LLMs Still Can't Plan; Can LRMs? A Preliminary Evaluation of OpenAI's o1 on PlanBench
finding: o1-preview is a poor judge of whether a planning goal is reachable. It usually hands back a plan for an impossible goal and sometimes calls solvable problems impossible.
numbers: 100 unsolvable and 600 solvable instances. Blocksworld: 27% of unsolvable instances correctly marked unsolvable, 19% returned an empty plan, 54% a full (impossible) plan; false 'unsolvable' on solvable instances 0%. Randomized Mystery Blocksworld: 16% correct, 5% empty plan, 79% full plan; false 'unsolvable' rate 11.5%. The authors note o1 sometimes gives a made-up reason for an impossible plan.
limits: Tests recognising unsolvability, not checking a given plan. 2024 model. Not a self-verification test.
agent_relevance: In 73% (Blocksworld) to 84% (Mystery Blocksworld) of impossible cases the model failed to flag impossibility. Keep a sound external plan validator in the loop for planning.

source: Pombal, Rei, Martins (2026) Self-Preference Bias in Rubric-Based Evaluation of Large Language Models
finding: On correctness-checked tasks (IFEval, LiveCodeBench), judges overrate their own outputs, including when each rubric is objective and ground truth is known. Self-recognition separates the effect cleanly; perplexity does not remove it.
numbers: 12 judges. LiveCodeBench: 177 problems, 5,685 tests as binary rubrics. Among rubrics where the generator fails, judges can be more than 50% more likely to mark them satisfied for their own output (abstract); worst case GPT-5 about 20 times more likely than for unrelated models. Table 22 (9 open-weight judges), ratio when the judge recognised the output as its own vs not: LiveCodeBench 1.88 vs 0.72; HealthBench 1.01 vs 0.78; IFEval 1.16 vs 1.09. Table 21: in the lowest-perplexity quartile the ratio stays above 1 on LiveCodeBench (1.48) and HealthBench (1.03) and is 0.94 on IFEval. Length: the ratio rises with own-output length quartile on LiveCodeBench (0.90, 3.12, 2.66, 5.32). Reasoning effort did not reduce self-preference on IFEval (Appendix G).
limits: Observational binning, not an intervention. The ratio is a risk ratio of false acceptance for self vs others, not an accuracy difference. Perplexity bins in the upper quartiles are unreliable because few self outputs land there. Recognition prompts a model to guess authorship, which can itself be noisy.
agent_relevance: Closes gap 6 in the direction that recognition is the stronger correlate on correctness tasks, with effect sizes. For the agent, use a checker from a different model family and do not let the same instance judge its own text without code or reference support.

source: Pombal, Rei, Martins (2026) Self-Preference Bias in Rubric-Based Evaluation (ensembling and paradigm comparison)
finding: A committee of judges from five families reduces self-preference but does not remove it. Self-preference is stronger in pairwise comparison than in rubric scoring.
numbers: Appendix F: on LiveCodeBench a majority-vote committee significantly reduces self-preference for four of five members; on IFEval the reductions are mostly negative in sign but not individually significant. Main text: SPB is significantly more severe in pairwise comparison than in rubric-based or direct assessment.
limits: The committee is made of the same families that appear as generators, so the test is lenient. Per-member effect sizes are in tables I did not copy.
agent_relevance: Mixed-family judging is the practical mitigation; asking a binary question per criterion is less biased than asking which of two is better.

source: Konstantinou, Tambon, Papadakis (2026) On the risk of coding before testing: an empirical study on LLM-based test generation workflow
finding: When a model writes tests after seeing faulty code, the tests copy the bug. Writing tests from the task description alone catches more faults. Chain-of-thought and chain-of-verification prompting do not fix it.
numbers: 5 models (GPT-5-mini, GPT-4.1-mini, DeepSeek-V4-Flash, Claude Haiku 4.5, Llama 3.3 70B), HumanEval+, MBPP, BigCodeBench. Fault detection 25% when tests are written independently vs 14% when written after faulty code. Showing the implementation under test cuts fault detection by 13.2% on average (per-model drops of 9.1, 15.2, 18.2 and 10.7 for four of the five models; the GPT-5 mini value was cut off in my text dump). Prompt-only beats summarization by 11.4 to 20.7 points, CoT by 9.5 to 25.8, and Chain-of-Verification by 7.6 to 16.7 across the five models. Test-first workflow beats agentic by 7.9 to 17.7 points.
limits: Faulty implementations were chosen to be hard (not caught by more than half of the reference tests). The paper measures fault detection, not an explicit correlation coefficient. Percent figures are as the paper reports them.
agent_relevance: Closes much of gap 4: the main driver of correlated error between code and its own tests is shared context (seeing the faulty solution), not only the shared model. Generate checks from the spec before, or without, seeing the candidate.

source: Leu, Oertel, Hebig (2026) Don't Bother to Use a Second LLM and Write Tests Yourself! A Study on Elixir
finding: For Elixir code, tests written by a different LLM than the code are no better at finding faults than tests written by the same LLM. Human-written tests found faults that all model-written tests missed.
numbers: 5 LLMs, 459 implementations and 2,709 test suites, 9,417 test-case failures analysed by hand. 247 implementations flagged as faulty; 99 of them were flagged only by manually written tests. No difference between same-model and different-model tests.
limits: Elixir is a rare language, so all models may share the same blind spots; the null result may reflect that. Not a measured error-correlation number. I read the abstract and introduction, not the full results section.
agent_relevance: Switching model family for the checker did not lower shared error here. Together with d18 this says: isolate context and use the spec, and do not count on a different vendor alone.

source: Stroebl, Kapoor, Narayanan (2024) Inference Scaling fLaws: The Limits of LLM Resampling with Imperfect Verifiers (re-opened)
finding: With an imperfect verifier the best number of tries is finite and small, because false positives rise with the number of attempts. The reason is task difficulty: easy tasks get solved early, and the tasks that remain are the ones where wrong answers pass the tests.
numbers: HumanEval+ and MBPP+. 200 samples per HumanEval task, resampled 1,000 times in random order. Cost-benefit ratio of a false positive to a true positive set to 0, 1, 2, 4, 8. At ratio 4, optimal K is about 5 for all four models; at ratio 10, optimal K is 0 for almost all models. Llama-3.1-70B has a false-positive rate that rises steeply with K; Code Llama and Command rise gradually, giving much higher optimal K, and the paper offers no explanation. Weaker models have more false positives, tied linearly to single-sample accuracy; no weaker model could match GPT-4o by resampling.
limits: Code tests as verifier; the difficulty distribution on HumanEval is bimodal. The paper gives no closed-form rule for K. From their expected-value setup (Appendix C), keep sampling while the chance that the next accepted answer is correct times its benefit exceeds the chance it is a false positive times its cost. That is my reading, not a stated rule.
agent_relevance: Partly answers gap 5: no simple empirical rule exists, but the stop rule is marginal and can be tuned by logging the accept rate and auditing a sample of accepted answers for false positives. Cap tries at about 5 unless the cost ratio is low or a stronger independent check exists.

source: Zeng et al. (2025) VersaPRM: Multi-Domain Process Reward Model via Synthetic Reasoning Data
finding: Math-trained process reward models give almost no gain over majority voting outside math. Training on synthetic multi-domain step labels restores a gain. Step-level scoring is not free outside its training domain.
numbers: MMLU-Pro subjects. Weighted majority voting gain over plain majority vote: Math +4.80 (Qwen-2.5-Math-PRM) and +1.73 (Math-Shepherd), Chemistry +2.00, Physics +3.34 (Math-Shepherd), Philosophy +0.34, History +0.20; 'All except math' maximum +0.71. VersaPRM: Law +7.9% over majority voting vs Qwen2.5-Math-PRM +1.3% (abstract). Held-out-domain ablation for law and biology: VersaPRM stays comparable to the fully trained model.
limits: Labels come from Llama-3.1-70B auto-labeling, so step correctness is machine-made. Evaluated on MMLU-Pro multiple choice, where chains are short and the answer space is small, so step-level vs answer-level checking is not cleanly separated from domain shift. Weighted majority voting with min-aggregation.
agent_relevance: Partly answers gap 7: out of domain, an off-the-shelf step-level scorer adds under 1 point over voting. Whether step checks add over answer checks in non-math domains has not been shown cleanly. Do not assume step-level checking transfers.

source: Zeng et al. (2025) VersaPRM (auto-labeler ablation: reference answer and step definitions)
finding: An LLM step labeler is only trustworthy when it is given a reference answer and written step definitions. Without them it flips most of its 'correct' labels.
numbers: Synthetic data: 5,750 MMLU-Pro questions, 16 chains each, 84,098 chains kept, 36,935 labelled error-free and 47,163 with at least one error. Re-labelling 30 questions with a simplified prompt (no step definitions, no ground-truth answer): agreement on chains first labelled correct fell by over 70 points to 7%; agreement on chains first labelled incorrect fell from 71% to 62%. A PRM trained on the ablated labels got under half the uplift over majority vote that the full-label PRM gets.
limits: Small audit set (30 questions). The reference here is the dataset's gold answer, not an independently sampled model answer, so it does not test gap 10 as posed.
agent_relevance: Supports giving a judge an answer key: a reference materially changes verdicts. It does not show that a sampled, possibly wrong, reference keeps the benefit.

source: Nitarach (2026) Model Capability Dominates: Inference-Time Optimization Lessons from AIMO 3
finding: For voting on 50 olympiad problems with gpt-oss-120b, prompt diversity did not decorrelate errors, because wrong answers already scatter; diversity only lowered accuracy. The gap to pass@20 is a selection loss that a verifier could close.
numbers: 3 models, 23+ experiments, 50 IMO-level problems. Method-of-moments pairwise correlation: all 19 computable estimates negative; seven with N of 7 or more averaged -0.122 (values -0.167 to -0.067); eleven N=3 points all -0.500 (the mathematical minimum); overall mean -0.348. Best majority-vote score 42/50 vs pass@20 mean 45.5. More prompt diversity monotonically lowered the score on gpt-oss-120b (N=21 baseline runs).
limits: The correlation estimate is on correct-vote counts with N from 3 to 16, so it is noisy and says wrong answers do not cluster, which is not the same as 'verifier errors are independent'. 50 problems, one competition. The paper did not test a verifier.
agent_relevance: Against gap 8: voting errors are not strongly correlated in this setting, so adding diverse prompts buys nothing, but a selector that beats the mode could still add up to about 3.5 of 50. Do not spend budget on prompt diversity for voters.

source: Sethi (2026) Don't Overthink It: Inter-Rollout Action Agreement as a Free Adaptive-Compute Signal for LLM Agents (TrACE)
finding: Sampling a few candidate answers and stopping early when they agree matched fixed-budget self-consistency with 33 to 65 percent fewer calls, with no learned difficulty predictor.
numbers: Qwen 2.5 3B Instruct on CPU. GSM8K (n=50) and MiniHouse (n=30, 15 steps, 3 seeds). TrACE-4 matches SC-4 with 33% fewer calls on GSM8K and 39% fewer on MiniHouse (15.07 vs 24.67 calls). TrACE-8 matches SC-8 (0.84 accuracy on GSM8K) with 55% fewer calls on GSM8K (3.56 vs 8.00) and 65% fewer on MiniHouse (16.27 vs 46.93). On MiniHouse, greedy is 0.367 and both SC-4 and SC-8 are 0.378, so extra samples barely help there.
limits: Very small samples (n=50, n=30); bootstrap CIs are wide (GSM8K greedy 0.78 [0.66, 0.88] vs SC-8 0.84 [0.74, 0.94]). 3B model. Single author. It compares to uniform SC, not to oracle difficulty.
agent_relevance: Cheap pilot agreement is a usable difficulty signal at least for a small model: ask 2 to 4 samples first, stop when they agree, add samples when they do not. It does not show routing between different methods (vote vs verify vs search), only how many samples to draw.

source: Liu et al. (2026) PETS: A Principled Framework Towards Optimal Trajectory Allocation for Efficient Test-Time Self-Consistency
finding: Adaptive allocation of samples across questions using agreement-based difficulty estimates beats uniform allocation. The target is agreement with the infinite-budget majority vote, not agreement with the true answer.
numbers: GPQA: perfect self-consistency (agreement with the infinite-budget majority) with up to 75% (offline) and 55% (online) smaller sampling budget than uniform. Tables compare to uniform and confidence-guided uniform on BRUMO and other datasets with 128 sampled traces, subsampled to 64, 30 repeats.
limits: The self-consistency rate measures agreement with the voting limit, not accuracy against truth, so gains apply only to the vote; if the vote is wrong the savings do not help. I read the abstract, introduction and part of the tables.
agent_relevance: Supports gap 9 for allocating samples across questions with cheap online agreement estimates. It leaves open routing between voting and verification.

source: Li et al. (2025) VerifyBench: A Systematic Benchmark for Evaluating Reasoning Verifiers Across Domains
finding: Reference-based answer checking by LLM judges is good in chemistry and biology and weaker in math and physics. Specialised verifiers have high accuracy but poor recall; general LLM judges have high recall but less stable precision. Input format changes results.
numbers: About 4,000 expert-level questions in math, physics, chemistry, biology; label split 45% correct / 55% incorrect. Best verifier accuracy 96.48% in chemistry, 89.16% in biology, 91.78% in physics; best overall accuracy 89.07% (xVerify-9B-C). General LLMs reach recall as high as 91.99% in math with lower precision, and some verifier cells in math are near 55% accuracy.
limits: This is reference-vs-response equivalence with the answer key supplied, not independent verification. Table cells are scrambled in my text extraction, so only the stated headline numbers are used.
agent_relevance: A judge with a reference is far more reliable where answers are short strings, and still weak on math expressions. Gap 10 remains open: no test here uses a sampled reference.

source: Singh et al. (2026) V1: Unifying Generation and Self-Verification for Parallel Reasoners
finding: Asking the model which of two candidate solutions is right (pairwise) is a more accurate self-verification than scoring each alone. A training-free tournament that gives more comparisons to the pairs it is least sure about raises Pass@1.
numbers: V1-Infer improves Pass@1 by up to 10% over pointwise verification on LiveCodeBench, CodeContests, SWE-Bench, AIME, HMMT; the V1-PairRL training variant adds 7 to 9% test-time scaling gains over standard RL. Self-aggregation methods suffered diversity collapse where Pass@N falls.
limits: I read the abstract and introduction, not the experiment tables, so per-benchmark numbers and the compute-matched comparison against majority voting are not confirmed. Code and math, where tests are available.
agent_relevance: Supports a pairwise check among the top two voted answers as the verification step: it avoids the miscalibration of absolute scores that Zhao saw (d02).

source: Setlur et al. (2025) Scaling Test-Time Compute Without Verification or RL is Suboptimal
finding: Proves that fine-tuning with a verifier (search or RL) beats distilling traces without one for a fixed budget, and that the gap widens with test-time budget when the base model's correct traces are heterogeneous and rewards are not sharply concentrated.
numbers: Experiments with 3B, 8B and 32B models on a didactic problem and math; Figure 1 compares S1-style supervised distillation to best-of-N with a verifier as budget grows. The gap increases with budget. Verifier test accuracy increases with training data (Figure 13).
limits: This is about training choices, not a scaffold-only agent, and the theory relies on an anti-concentration condition measured in Figure 10. I read the abstract, intro and appendix headings, not the proofs.
agent_relevance: Weak support for spending budget on verification as runs get long; it does not say a prompted verifier on a frozen model has the same property.
